fun_highlights: Callback cards are the game at its best: the lonely child who becomes a patron, the scholar's bet paying off decades later, the book re-read at midlife. These deliver genuine narrative surprise and closure within a single life.

The four-calling fork (soldier / scholar / maker / wanderer) plus era-gating creates structurally distinct adult arcs — a soldier born into a war year gets vx_soldier_war, a scholar in a turning age gets vx_scholar_turning. This is real content differentiation, not just text flavour.
The motto crystallization moment is genuinely satisfying: watching a reputation build across 3-4 generations toward words the family can live by is the dynasty layer working as intended.

Heirlooms carry meaning: 'the book too hard for a child's hands' reappearing at cb_books_late, read by the third or fourth heir who actually traces it to the ancestor who kept it, is the kind of cross-generational texture that makes the dynasty system worth building.

The bequest card (e_bequest) is a real lever — choosing 'everything I know' vs. 'every coin I can spare' vs. 'their own freedom' produces meaningfully different heir starting conditions, and the heir screen names the choice explicitly. As a dynasty player, this is the one moment I feel agency across the generation boundary.
The seat-gated and repute-gated cards (r_scholar_door, r_hard_name, s_patronage, s_great_burden) give genuine dynasty-tier payoffs — content that a low-seat house simply never sees.

Era variety is real: plague, war, hard years, plenty, and the turning age each produce distinct opening circumstances and gate distinct events. Dynasty 8 (Vane) born into 'turning' reads differently from Dynasty 9 (Bjornsen) born into 'hard years'.
staleness: The reckoning (x_reckoning) — the one explicitly adversarial dynasty event — does not fire in any of the 15 dynasties in the transcript. Not once across 30+ individual lives, including several that reach seat 3-6. For a dynasty-strategist this is the moment: 'a debt called in, a name questioned.' Its absence means the downside risk of holding a great seat is never felt. The code requires seat>=3 and cool:16 and fires during ages 30-80; the likely cause is a cooldown-vs-lifespan mismatch or seats rarely staying above 3 long enough before the player's eligible age window. Either way, the player never faces the reckoning, which hollows the dynasty's tension.

The love-marry-child sequence is structurally monotonous. Across 15 dynasties, the dominant pattern is: love arrives late (30s-50s via a_meet_late), marriage follows, child arrives near the window's end or not at all. The code added spread mechanisms but the transcripts show it clustering. By dynasty 6 the player knows this beat is coming and it has stopped being discovery. A dynasty strategist wants to plan around heirs — the heir is mechanically important — but the when and whether feel out of their hands in a way that doesn't feel like meaningful uncertainty, just pattern.

Body-aging observation lines repeat across every late-life within a session. 'Some mornings the body answers the bell late,' 'The body keeps its own ledger now,' 'Mornings take longer to arrive in the body' — multiple variants of the same image land in nearly every life that passes 55, and across 15 dynasties they become a familiar texture rather than a fresh one. The freshPick() pool for aging observations is smaller than for other categories and it shows.

The y_calling card has only three prompt variants and four fixed options. By dynasty 4 the player knows: here comes the fork. It has stopped being a fork in a life and become a form to fill. The 'structural moment' that is supposed to differentiate adult arcs is itself one of the most predictable beats in the game.

The secret and tainted reputation track is nearly invisible in play. The cb_inherited_secret fires once in 15 dynasties, r_old_shame and r_family_shadow do not appear at all. A dynasty that deliberately pursues the 'tainted' reputation path — one of the nine available — gets almost nothing back from it in terms of distinctive content. The shadow track is the least developed of the reputation arcs.

Seat climbing is mechanically opaque and non-interactive for most of a life. m_invest_name (the deliberate lever) fires rarely in the transcripts; the seat mostly moves on peakMeans thresholds the player cannot directly see or control. A dynasty strategist wants to know: what can I do THIS generation to move the house? Outside the bequest and the invest-in-name card, the answer is largely 'play well and hope,' which dulls the strategic layer.

improvements.what: Fix the reckoning's firing rate for seat-3+ houses. Audit the cooldown-vs-lifespan arithmetic: with cool:16 and an eligible window of 30-80, a life that reaches seat 3 at gen 2 and lives 65 years should see it at least once. Consider dropping cool to 12, widening the eligible age window, or adding a guaranteed-fire trigger when a house has been at seat>=3 for two consecutive generations without facing it.
improvements.why: The reckoning is the only card that applies real downside pressure to a high-standing house. Without it, the dynasty layer has no adversarial tension — you climb and you stay climbed, which removes the strategic interest of protecting what you've built.

improvements.what: Give the dynasty-strategist two or three more direct levers per generation: a 'commit to an alliance' card that boosts seat probability next gen but costs means this gen; a 'groom the heir' card that improves the bequest effects if taken before e_bequest; or a 'burn the bridges' ruthless-investment card distinct from m_invest_name. The point is predictable, plannable agency: I did X this generation TO SET UP Y next generation.
improvements.why: Right now the only truly cross-generational player lever is e_bequest (mind/means/heart/free). More levers would make the dynasty feel steerable rather than witnessed.

improvements.what: Expand and differentiate the body-aging observation pool, or gate body lines behind vocation/trait/stat so they read distinctly per character. A frail scholar's late years should feel different from a soldier's. The current pool is smaller than other observation categories and the same images recur across every long life in a session.
improvements.why: The ambient observations are the primary texture of years-without-cards. When they repeat across 10 consecutive lives they stop being texture and become wallpaper.

improvements.what: Enrich the tainted/secret reputation track with 2-3 more repute-gated cards so a house that deliberately builds a 'we do not speak of everything' identity gets distinctive content. Currently r_old_shame and r_family_shadow exist but never appeared in 15 dynasties; add at least one guaranteed-fire 'shadow card' when a house has held the tainted reputation for 2+ generations.
improvements.why: The tainted/secret path is one of nine available reputation arcs but has the thinnest content. A dynasty player who chose to cultivate it gets no payoff.

improvements.what: Vary the y_calling prompt more radically by era and house-seat. A child born into a great house in a war era should face a meaningfully different version of the fork than a landless founder in settled times. The current three variants are structurally identical — same prose rhythm, same four options. Era-specific calling text (or at minimum, seat-specific framing for the high-seat variant) would make this inevitable beat feel fresh longer.
improvements.why: The calling card is the most predictable moment in every life; it's also supposed to be the structural fork that makes lives different. It can carry more of that work.

verdict: As a dynasty strategist the game offers a genuinely interesting skeleton — mottos, heirlooms, the bequest lever, seat-gated content — but the reckoning never fires, the direct levers are thin, and by dynasty 6 the life-template (late love, calling fork, body-aging observations) is familiar enough that I'm watching the house accrue standing rather than steering it.
